UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms  
 
 
        Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
PRE-FILED STATEMENT OF PAMELA QUINLAN 
 PRINCIPAL, GQS NEW ENERGY STRATEGIES 
 
Preserving the Regional Compact: Governance, Accountability, and Resource Adequacy in 
PJM's Next Phase of Evolution 
Chairman Swett and Commissioners Rosner, See, Chang, and LaCerte: 
Thank you for the opportunity to participate in this technical conference. I appreciate the 
Commission's decision to convene this discussion at a time when PJM is confronting some of the 
most significant operational, market, and reliability challenges in its history. 
My name is Pamela Quinlan. I am a Principal and Co-Founder of GQS New Energy Strategies. I 
am participating today in my personal capacity, and the views expressed in this statement are my 
own and do not reflect the views of my clients. 
I have participated on PJM matters from a number of different perspectives for the past two 
decades. I first became involved in PJM in 2005 while working for one of the early competitive 
demand response providers. I later represented Rockland Electric Company as a voting member 
of PJM's Transmission Owner Sector. I subsequently served at the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission as an Energy Industry Analyst, Technical Advisor to Commissioner Rich Glick, as 
well as Chief of Staff. During my time at the Commission, I worked on numerous rulemakings, 
proceedings and technical conferences involving various aspects of PJM's market design, 
transmission planning, and resource adequacy. Today, as a consultant, I advise a broad range of 
market participants—including utilities, transmission developers, generation developers, storage 
developers and large electricity customers investing billions of dollars across the PJM footprint. 
Those experiences have provided a unique vantage point from which to observe PJM's evolution. 
They have also led me to one consistent conclusion: every constituency believes PJM's 
governance process is not working for them. 
Suppliers have argued that stakeholder processes move too slowly to respond to changing market 
conditions. Consumer advocates have argued that markets fail to adequately protect customers. 
States have expressed frustration that regional institutions are insufficiently responsive to state 
policy objectives. Transmission owners, public power entities, large end use customers,

environmental organizations have all, at different times, concluded that PJM's governance 
structure is contributing to the challenges confronting the region. 
The consistency of those criticisms is striking. When every constituency believes the system is 
working against it, the natural instinct is to conclude that the governance model itself is broken. 
I am not convinced that is the correct or complete diagnosis. 
PJM unquestionably faces serious challenges. It was slow to modernize its generation 
interconnection process, slower than many of its peers to embrace forward-looking transmission 
planning, and unprepared for the unprecedented pace of large-load growth now reshaping the 
region. Those shortcomings contributed directly to today's resource adequacy concerns, even as 
PJM has more recently undertaken significant reforms to address them.  
At the same time, electricity demand is increasing at a pace not experienced in decades, while the 
infrastructure necessary to support that growth has become increasingly difficult and time-
consuming to develop. Importantly, the region's greatest constraint today is not a lack of 
commercial interest or private capital. Billions of dollars are prepared to be invested in new 
generation, transmission, storage, and large load development.  
The defining constraint on the electric system today is infrastructure: our collective ability to site 
it, permit it, interconnect it, finance it, and build it quickly enough to maintain reliability. 
No governance reform, market design, or resource adequacy construct will succeed unless the 
institutions responsible for planning and developing that infrastructure are capable of working 
together effectively. Those challenges deserve the Commission's attention, and governance 
reform can undoubtedly improve how PJM responds to them. But governance is only part of the 
story. 
Increasingly, the decisions that create new reliability obligations are made by institutions outside 
PJM's direct control, while PJM remains responsible for maintaining reliability across one of the 
largest synchronized electric systems in the world. The recent resource adequacy challenges 
confronting PJM did not cause this disconnect. They revealed it. The institutions creating new 
reliability obligations are increasingly different from the institutions responsible for ensuring 
those obligations can be met. State legislators, Governors and commissions make policy 
decisions that either advance or halt new load, generation, supply, and transmission. Governance 
reforms can improve PJM’s decision-making, but they cannot, by themselves, resolve that 
growing disconnect. In my view, aligning authority, responsibility, and accountability across the 
regional compact is the central challenge confronting PJM today.  
The objective of this proceeding, therefore, should not simply be to improve PJM's governance. 
It should be to preserve and strengthen the regional compact that has made PJM one of the 
nation's most successful electric institutions.

Regional coordination remains one of the greatest achievements of modern electricity policy. 
Through coordinated system operations, regional transmission planning, competitive wholesale 
markets, and security-constrained economic dispatch, PJM has delivered substantial economic 
and reliability benefits to the 67 million consumers across thirteen states and the District of 
Columbia. Those benefits become even more valuable as electricity demand accelerates, resource 
portfolios diversify, and the bulk power system grows more complex. 
Ultimately, the purpose of preserving the regional compact is to preserve the reliable and 
affordable electric service those institutions were created to deliver. Reliability and affordability 
are too often treated as competing objectives when durable affordability depends upon 
maintaining a reliable electric system supported by adequate infrastructure and timely 
investment. Consumers bear the costs of inadequate planning and resource shortages just as 
surely as they bear the costs of unnecessary investment. The challenge before the Commission is 
to ensure that the institutions supporting the regional compact can deliver both.  
Meeting that challenge requires more than governance reform alone. It requires stronger 
institutional leadership, a more clearly defined partnership between PJM and the states, and a 
renewed focus on aligning responsibility for creating reliability obligations with accountability 
for meeting them.  
This statement offers six principal observations. 
1. The regional compact remains fundamentally sound and should be strengthened rather 
than weakened. 
2. Many of PJM's recent challenges were preceded by failures of strategic long-term 
planning and institutional adaptation rather than defects inherent in the governance model 
itself. 
3. PJM does not principally lack legal authority. It lacks the institutional confidence to 
exercise the authority it already possesses. Governance reform should therefore focus less 
on expanding legal authorities and more on empowering an independent Board to 
establish priorities, manage the stakeholder process, make difficult decisions, and 
exercise its expert judgment when consensus cannot be achieved.  
4. States should be recognized as institutional partners, not merely stakeholders, with a 
defined role in the development of long-term planning and resource adequacy initiatives. 
States occupy a unique constitutional and regulatory role. They determine where 
generation and transmission facilities may be built, regulate the utilities responsible for 
serving retail customers, and increasingly shape the economic development and resource 
policy decisions that drive future reliability needs. That partnership should begin earlier, 
be more strategic, and be supported by the technical resources necessary for states to 
participate effectively, while allowing each state to determine how it wishes to be 
represented.

5. The next evolution of resource adequacy should better align responsibility for serving 
load with responsibility for demonstrating that sufficient accredited resources exist to 
support that load.  
6. Finally, governance reform should be evaluated not by whether it redistributes influence 
among stakeholders, but by whether it strengthens the regional institutions that 
consumers increasingly depend upon.  
The recommendations that follow are offered in that spirit. 
 
Preserving the Regional Compact 
The debate over PJM's future should begin with a simple question: Why does the regional 
compact exist in the first place?  Recent discussions have understandably questioned whether 
PJM has become too large, too complex, or too difficult to govern effectively. Those concerns 
deserve careful consideration. But they should not cause us to lose sight of the extraordinary 
benefits that regional coordination has delivered, or assume that today's challenges demonstrate 
that the regional model itself has reached its limits.  
PJM was never intended to replace the authority of states, utilities, or private investment. Rather, 
it was created because certain functions are performed more cost-effectively at a regional scale 
than they can be by individual utilities or states acting alone. Its success has always depended on 
each institution performing the responsibilities that only it can perform. Operating an 
interconnected bulk power system, dispatching generation economically across multiple 
jurisdictions, planning transmission over a broad geographic footprint, and administering 
competitive wholesale markets all produce benefits that no single state or utility could achieve 
independently. 
Every day, PJM coordinates the operation of generating units across thirteen states and the 
District of Columbia. Through security-constrained economic dispatch, it continuously selects 
the lowest-cost combination of available resources capable of serving demand while respecting 
the physical limitations of the transmission system. Regional transmission planning recognizes 
that reliability challenges do not stop at state boundaries, allowing infrastructure to be developed 
where it provides the greatest overall benefit rather than where individual jurisdictions happen to 
exercise authority. Competitive wholesale markets likewise benefit from regional scale by 
supporting greater liquidity, broader competition, and more efficient investment than would be 
possible in a collection of fragmented balancing authorities. 
The scale of PJM is therefore not an accident. It is one of its greatest strengths. A larger footprint 
allows operators to share reserves across a wider geographic area, dispatch a broader and 
increasingly diverse resource portfolio, respond more effectively to extreme weather, and 
maintain reliability at lower overall cost than would otherwise be possible. As electricity demand

accelerates, weather patterns become more volatile, and resource portfolios continue to diversify, 
those regional benefits become increasingly important. 
None of that means PJM should operate exactly as it did twenty years ago. The electric system 
has changed dramatically. Load is growing at rates not seen in decades. Data centers and other 
large industrial facilities are developing on timelines that frequently outpace traditional utility 
planning cycles. Generation, transmission, and natural gas infrastructure take longer to permit, 
interconnect, and construct. States are pursuing increasingly diverse policy objectives, while new 
technologies are transforming both the supply and demand sides of the electric system. Those 
changes require the institutions supporting the regional compact to evolve. 
That need for institutional evolution, however, should not be mistaken for evidence that regional 
coordination itself has failed. Quite the opposite. The more dynamic and interconnected the 
electric system becomes, the greater the value of regional coordination. The question before the 
Commission is therefore not whether PJM is too large to function. It is whether the institutions 
supporting the regional compact have evolved quickly enough to govern a much larger, faster-
moving, and more complex electric system. In my view, they have not. But that is an argument 
for strengthening the regional compact, not abandoning it. The challenge is not that regional 
markets have outlived their usefulness. It is that governance, planning, accountability, and 
institutional coordination have not kept pace with the profound changes occurring across the 
electric sector. The sections that follow explain why I believe stronger Board leadership, a more 
meaningful partnership with the states, and clearer accountability for resource adequacy provide 
a more durable path than weakening the regional model that has served consumers so well for 
more than two decades.  
 
How PJM Fell Behind 
None of this is to suggest that PJM has not made important mistakes. It has. Acknowledging 
those mistakes is important because they contributed directly to many of the challenges 
confronting the region today. At the same time, it is equally important to distinguish between 
those mistakes and the broader institutional questions now before the Commission. Better 
governance alone would not necessarily have prevented them, nor will correcting them alone 
prepare PJM for the electric system that is emerging. 
The common thread running through many of PJM's recent challenges is not poor governance, 
but delayed institutional adaptation. As the electric system changed, PJM was often slower than 
the pace of that change. Three examples illustrate the point. 
First, PJM waited too long to modernize its generation interconnection process. While other 
regional transmission organizations transitioned earlier to cluster studies and more forward-
looking queue management, PJM continued to rely on a serial interconnection process that 
became increasingly unworkable as project volumes accelerated. By the time comprehensive

reforms were adopted, the backlog had grown so large that PJM ultimately paused new 
interconnection requests for several years while implementing a new framework. That pause 
occurred at precisely the moment electricity demand began accelerating, delaying the 
interconnection and availability of new resources when they were becoming most needed. The 
region continues to feel the effects of that delay. 
Second, PJM was slower than many of its peers to fully embrace long-term, forward-looking 
planning. Historically, its planning processes excelled at identifying and correcting discrete 
reliability violations on the existing system in the near-term. As the electric sector evolved, 
however, planning increasingly required anticipating where the system was heading rather than 
simply responding to where it had been. PJM is in the midst of substantial progress through 
capacity expansion modeling, Order No. 1920 adoption, and more comprehensive assessments of 
transmission and generation needs. Those reforms represent meaningful progress, but they 
arrived only after the underlying trends had already begun reshaping the region. 
Finally, the explosive growth in large electricity demand exposed shortcomings in PJM's 
forecasting assumptions. No forecasting process will perfectly anticipate disruptive change, but 
the warning signs surrounding accelerating data center development and other large industrial 
loads emerged over a number of years. Earlier recognition of those trends could have prompted 
earlier transmission planning, earlier consideration of resource adequacy reforms, and earlier 
coordination among PJM, the states, utilities, and market participants. PJM's recent reforms, 
including independent validation of large-load forecasts and more rigorous review of utility 
submissions, are important improvements that should significantly strengthen planning going 
forward. 
These were meaningful mistakes, and they deserve acknowledgment. But I do not believe they 
fully explain PJM's current predicament, nor do I believe different governance alone would 
necessarily have prevented them. Institutions often struggle to recognize structural change while 
it is occurring, particularly when that change accelerates rapidly. 
The recent surge in electricity demand did not create the disconnect now confronting PJM. It 
revealed it. For many years, relatively stable demand growth and comfortable reserve margins 
allowed the region to absorb institutional misalignment without immediate reliability 
consequences. Today's resource adequacy challenges have exposed that those margins no longer 
exist. Increasingly, questions involving governance, planning, market design, and stakeholder 
processes are all converging on a single structural issue: who is ultimately responsible for 
ensuring that sufficient infrastructure and accredited resources exist to serve future load. 
That is the challenge the remaining sections of this statement seek to address. They focus less on 
correcting yesterday's mistakes than on preparing PJM for tomorrow's electric system by 
strengthening institutional leadership, creating a more meaningful partnership with the states, 
and restoring clearer accountability for resource adequacy. None of those recommendations

requires abandoning the regional compact. To the contrary, each is intended to strengthen it by 
ensuring that every institution performs the responsibilities it is uniquely positioned to carry out. 
 
What Governance Can—and Cannot—Fix 
The Commission has convened this technical conference to consider whether reforms to PJM's 
governance and stakeholder processes are necessary. I believe that question is both timely and 
important because governance matters. The way institutions make decisions affects not only the 
quality of those decisions, but whether they are made early enough to avoid crises. Good 
governance cannot guarantee good outcomes, but it can improve an institution's ability to 
recognize change, establish priorities, and act before emerging challenges become reliability 
problems. 
That is particularly important today because the defining challenge facing the electric system is 
no longer simply attracting investment. It is ensuring that the infrastructure necessary to support 
that investment is planned, permitted, interconnected, and constructed before reliability needs 
arise. Markets remain extraordinarily effective at allocating capital. They are far less effective at 
overcoming delays in permitting, siting, transmission development, and interconnection. Those 
challenges require earlier planning, stronger institutional coordination, and clearer accountability 
across the regional compact. 
Governance has an important role to play in meeting that challenge, but it should not become a 
catch-all explanation for every challenge confronting the region. Good governance should 
produce institutions that anticipate change rather than react to it. It should encourage long-term 
planning instead of crisis management, establish clear priorities, and provide decision-makers 
with the confidence to act before reliability is threatened. It cannot, however, eliminate the 
physical, economic, and jurisdictional realities that ultimately determine whether sufficient 
infrastructure can be developed to meet future demand. 
Many of the decisions that shape future reliability occur outside PJM. Utilities undertake new 
obligations to serve load. States establish resource policies and promote economic development. 
Local governments determine whether transmission and generation infrastructure can be sited 
and permitted. Private developers decide when projects move forward. PJM must then forecast 
demand, plan transmission, administer markets, and maintain reliability after many of those 
decisions have already been made. Governance can improve how PJM responds to those 
realities. It cannot substitute for earlier planning, stronger institutional coordination, or clearer 
accountability for the decisions that create future reliability obligations. 
Viewed through that lens, the challenge confronting PJM is not simply that decisions take too 
long. It is that the pace of change affecting the electric system has begun to outstrip the 
institutional mechanisms through which those changes are identified, evaluated, and acted upon. 
The answer is therefore not to abandon stakeholder governance, nor to centralize every important

decision within the PJM Board. It is to ensure that governance is used for the purpose for which 
it is best suited: establishing strategic direction, identifying emerging risks early, aligning the 
institutions responsible for reliability, and enabling timely action before reliability challenges 
become crises. 
That naturally leads to the next question: if governance is intended to provide strategic leadership 
rather than solve every operational challenge, how should responsibility be shared between the 
Board and the stakeholder process? 
 
Leadership, Consensus, and the Role of the Board 
Much of the discussion surrounding PJM governance has focused on two related questions: Has 
the stakeholder process become too slow? And should the Board exercise greater authority? Both 
are appropriate questions, but I do not believe they fully capture the issue confronting PJM 
today. The more fundamental question is whether PJM is using the right governance process for 
the type of decision it is trying to make. 
One of PJM's greatest institutional strengths has always been its commitment to an open, 
transparent, consensus-based stakeholder process. Few organizations are able to bring together 
the breadth of operational, engineering, market, regulatory, and commercial expertise that exists 
within PJM's membership. That collaborative process has consistently produced better tariffs, 
stronger implementation, and more durable reforms than would likely emerge from a purely top-
down regulatory approach. It should remain one of PJM's defining characteristics. 
At the same time, not every issue benefits from the same governance model. Technical questions 
involving Manuals, market mechanics, operational procedures, and implementation details 
benefit enormously from extensive stakeholder engagement because the objective is to improve 
the quality of implementation. Strategic questions are different. Decisions involving resource 
adequacy, transmission planning, market design, and emerging reliability risks require balancing 
competing public interests, establishing institutional priorities, and determining how much risk 
the region is willing to accept. Those are not simply technical questions, nor are they questions 
that can always be resolved through negotiation among stakeholders whose commercial interests 
are directly affected by the outcome.  
That distinction explains why consensus and leadership serve different, but complementary, 
purposes. Consensus is exceptionally effective at improving solutions. Leadership defines the 
problem to be solved, establishes the objectives that must be achieved, and determines when 
action is necessary.  
It should therefore not be surprising that consensus becomes increasingly difficult when 
stakeholders are asked to redesign the very markets in which they participate. That is not 
necessarily a failure of the stakeholder process. Rather, it reflects the reality that stakeholders

with fundamentally different interests will not always agree on questions involving the allocation 
of costs, risks, and opportunities. Those are precisely the circumstances in which Board 
leadership becomes most important.   
Recognizing those distinct roles, I believe the Board should lead on direction while stakeholders 
should lead on design. The Board should define the problem requiring resolution, establish the 
objectives any solution must satisfy, set an appropriate timeframe for action, and identify where 
stakeholder expertise is most valuable. Stakeholders should then do what they do best: improve 
proposals, evaluate alternatives, identify operational concerns, and build consensus wherever 
consensus can reasonably be achieved.  
This distinction also informs the current discussion regarding Section 205 filing rights. 
Considerable attention has been given to whether PJM should possess broader Section 205 
authority, whether the Board should have additional filing rights over matters currently governed 
by the Operating Agreement, or whether states should possess greater authority to initiate 
Commission action. These are thoughtful questions, and there may well be merit in considering 
targeted changes over time. I am not persuaded, however, that they address PJM’s principal 
challenge. 
The region's most pressing challenge today is resource adequacy. Yet the Board already 
possesses broad Section 205 authority over the capacity market and many of the reforms 
necessary to address that challenge. Where the Board concludes that changes are needed in areas 
where PJM does not possess unilateral Section 205 filing authority, it retains the ability to seek 
relief from this Commission under Section 206 when it believes existing tariff provisions have 
become unjust, unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory. The limiting factor has therefore not 
been the absence of legal authority. It has been the willingness to exercise the authority that 
already exists.  
Over time, stakeholder consensus has increasingly come to be viewed as a prerequisite for action 
rather than an important input into institutional judgment. Consensus should remain the preferred 
outcome wherever it can reasonably be achieved because reforms developed collaboratively are 
often stronger, more durable, and easier to implement. But consensus is a means of improving 
decisions; it should not become a prerequisite for exercising judgment. 
An independent Board is valuable only if its independence produces leadership. The purpose of 
an independent Board is not to insulate its members from disagreement or controversy. It is to 
enable them to exercise their expert judgment when consensus cannot be achieved and difficult 
decisions nevertheless must be made.  
Once the Board concludes that action is necessary to preserve reliability or maintain just and 
reasonable rates, it should be prepared to exercise the authorities already available to it. 
Consensus should remain the preferred outcome, but it should not become a justification for 
inaction. When meaningful stakeholder engagement has occurred and the Board concludes that

change remains necessary, exercising its existing authority—including seeking Commission 
action under Section 206 where appropriate—is not a failure of the stakeholder process. It is the 
governance model functioning as intended. 
Recent Board elections suggest that stakeholders increasingly express dissatisfaction with 
substantive policy outcomes through the election process. Accountability to stakeholders remains 
an important feature of PJM's governance, but accountability should not come at the expense of 
independence. PJM should therefore consider whether longer Board terms, coupled with the 
expectation that Board members generally serve a single term, would better balance 
accountability with the independence necessary to exercise expert judgment. 
Twenty years ago, waiting another six months for consensus often carried relatively modest 
consequences. Today's system is fundamentally different. Infrastructure takes longer to develop, 
electricity demand is growing more rapidly, reserve margins are tighter, and the margin for error 
has narrowed considerably. As the cost of institutional delay continues to rise, the value of an 
independent Board lies not simply in its independence, but in its willingness to exercise 
independent judgment. That is the form of leadership the next era of regional coordination will 
require. 
 
The States as Partners in Reliability 
The Commission has appropriately asked whether states should play a larger role in PJM's 
governance and whether additional procedural rights or filing authorities are necessary to ensure 
that regional markets remain responsive to state priorities. In my view, the more important 
question is not whether states should have greater influence within PJM's governance structure. 
It is whether the institutions responsible for solving the region's most pressing reliability 
challenges are working together early enough, and with sufficient shared accountability, to 
develop durable solutions. 
States are fundamentally different from other PJM stakeholders. They are sovereign governments 
exercising authorities that PJM neither has nor should have. States determine where generation 
and transmission facilities may be built. They regulate the utilities responsible for serving retail 
customers. They oversee resource planning in many jurisdictions and increasingly influence 
where new economic development—including large industrial facilities and data centers—
occurs. Those decisions directly shape both electricity demand and the infrastructure available to 
meet it. 
PJM's responsibility is equally unique. It must forecast those developments, determine what 
infrastructure and resources will be required, operate the regional transmission system reliably, 
and administer wholesale markets that support efficient investment.

This division of responsibilities is not new. It is the foundation of the cooperative federalism 
upon which organized wholesale markets have always depended. 
What has changed is the environment in which those responsibilities are exercised. 
For much of PJM's history, the region benefited from relatively modest load growth, stronger 
reserve margins, and sufficient flexibility within the system that imperfect coordination among 
institutions could often be absorbed without immediate reliability consequences. Today, we are 
operating under very different conditions. Electricity demand is increasing at rates not 
experienced in decades. Infrastructure takes significantly longer to permit and construct. Reserve 
margins are tighter, and the consequences of inaccurate planning or delayed investment are felt 
much more quickly. 
As the margin for error narrows, coordination among institutions becomes substantially more 
important. 
Resource adequacy provides perhaps the clearest example. Reliable service depends on 
competitive markets producing efficient investment signals. It depends on timely development of 
generation and transmission infrastructure. It depends on utility planning, state permitting and 
siting decisions, and economic development policies that recognize the infrastructure necessary 
to support new load. No single institution controls all of these decisions, yet each institution 
influences the outcome. 
This also requires recognizing the relationship between affordability and investment. 
States quite appropriately seek to protect consumers from unnecessary cost increases. PJM 
appropriately relies on competitive markets to signal when additional resources are needed. Both 
objectives are legitimate. But they cannot be pursued in isolation. Markets cannot be expected to 
attract the investment necessary to address resource shortages if scarcity prices are consistently 
moderated without corresponding actions to accelerate the infrastructure needed to relieve those 
shortages. Likewise, stronger market signals alone cannot solve reliability challenges if new 
infrastructure cannot be sited, permitted, or constructed in a timely manner. 
The answer is not to choose between affordability and investment, or between state authority and 
regional markets. The answer is to better integrate those decisions before they become crises. 
That is why I believe the relationship between PJM and the states should evolve beyond 
consultation toward shared accountability for those initiatives that inherently require both 
regional and state action. 
Today, the states already engage regularly with PJM through the Organization of PJM States, Inc. 
(OPSI). Those discussions are valuable and should continue. The issue is not that the states lack 
access or that PJM is unwilling to listen. Rather, the governance structure does not adequately 
recognize that success on many of today's most important issues ultimately depends on actions

that only the states can take. Influence alone is not enough when implementation requires shared 
ownership of the solution. 
Accordingly, I believe major initiatives involving long-term transmission planning, resource 
adequacy, and other issues that directly implicate state authorities should be developed by PJM 
in collaboration with a standing committee of state representatives before entering the 
stakeholder process. I do not believe the Commission or PJM should prescribe who represents 
each state. That decision should remain with the states themselves. Depending on the issue, a 
public utility commission, governor's office, energy office, or another designated entity may be 
the most appropriate representative. 
If states are expected to assume a more strategic role, they must also have the institutional 
capacity to fulfill it. These issues are extraordinarily technical, requiring expertise in engineering, 
economics, market design, and transmission planning. Other regions have recognized this need 
by providing states with the budget for independent technical support.1 PJM should consider 
similar approaches so that states have the professional resources necessary to participate as 
effective partners in developing long-term regional strategies. 
None of this should diminish PJM's responsibility or the authority of its Board. PJM must remain 
wholly responsible for determining what reliability requires and for making the regional 
decisions necessary to preserve the integrity of the interconnected system. Shared accountability 
does not mean shared veto authority. It means recognizing that regional strategies are more likely 
to succeed when the institutions responsible for implementing them help develop them from the 
outset. 
Viewed through that lens, the question is not whether states should have a larger seat at the table. 
It is whether the institutions whose decisions collectively determine reliability are organized in a 
way that allows them to solve increasingly complex problems together. As the electric system 
continues to evolve and the margin for error continues to narrow, I believe the answer must 
increasingly be yes. That partnership should not end with consultation. Its purpose is to restore 
accountability for resource adequacy by aligning the institutions that create new reliability 
obligations with those responsible for ensuring they can be met.  
 
Restoring Accountability for Resource Adequacy 
The discussion above ultimately points to what I believe is the central institutional question 
confronting PJM. If resource adequacy is increasingly shaped by decisions made across multiple 
institutions, then the question is no longer simply how PJM procures capacity. The question is

assets/documents/100026/1a_nescoe_2026_budget.pdf (setting forth NESCOE’s annual operating budget, including 
funding for professional staff and technical, legal, and consulting support provided on behalf of the New England 
states in regional electricity matters).

whether responsibility for creating new reliability obligations remains aligned with responsibility 
for ensuring those obligations can be met.  
The Reliability Pricing Model provides a useful illustration of why the region's resource 
adequacy framework must evolve. RPM was developed during a period of relatively stable 
demand growth, shorter infrastructure development timelines, and a market in which the Base 
Residual Auction was intended to function largely as a residual procurement mechanism. 
Bilateral contracting, self-supply, and other forward procurement activities were expected to 
satisfy much of the region's resource adequacy needs, with the auction procuring only the 
remaining capacity necessary to maintain reliability. 
That is no longer how the market functions. 
Today, the overwhelming majority of capacity clears through the centralized auction. More 
importantly, the auction has increasingly become the institution expected to reconcile decisions 
made by others. New wholesale load is added through utility service obligations and competitive 
retail arrangements without any corresponding requirement that the entity undertaking that 
obligation demonstrate how it intends to secure the accredited resources necessary to serve that 
load. States likewise make decisions regarding economic development, environmental policy, 
and the future composition of the generation fleet pursuant to their own statutory responsibilities. 
Those decisions are entirely appropriate exercises of state authority. But they also have direct 
implications for regional resource adequacy. If a state encourages significant new electricity 
demand or adopts policies that accelerate the retirement of existing resources, there should also 
be a credible strategy for ensuring that sufficient replacement resources and supporting 
infrastructure will be available when they are needed.  
Even if scarcity prices were allowed to fully reflect market conditions, price signals alone cannot 
solve what has become fundamentally a planning and accountability challenge. Scarcity pricing 
may indicate that additional resources are needed, but it cannot shorten permitting timelines, 
accelerate transmission construction, resolve interconnection delays, or eliminate the uncertainty 
associated with developing major infrastructure. Generation, transmission, and natural gas 
infrastructure frequently require five to ten years—or longer—to finance, permit, interconnect, 
and construct. By contrast, the Base Residual Auction provides a single year of revenue 
guaranteed only a few years before delivery. That mismatch between investment timelines and 
market timelines has become increasingly significant. 
The issue, therefore, is not whether competitive markets have failed. It is that we have 
increasingly asked the centralized capacity market to solve problems it was never designed to 
solve. 
At its core, this reflects a broader shift in the nature of the resource adequacy challenge. When 
RPM was developed, the principal question was whether markets would produce sufficient 
investment in new generation. Today, the greater challenge is whether the infrastructure

necessary to support that investment can be planned, permitted, interconnected, and constructed 
before reliability needs arise. Competitive markets remain highly effective at allocating capital 
among competing resources. They are far less capable of coordinating the planning, permitting, 
siting, and long-term infrastructure development that increasingly determine whether those 
resources can reach commercial operation when they are needed. Resource adequacy has 
therefore become as much an infrastructure and institutional coordination challenge as it is a 
market challenge.  
That shift has also placed increasing pressure on PJM's governance. As long as the region 
continues to rely on the centralized capacity market to reconcile structural issues that originate 
elsewhere, participants will continue to debate market rules in an effort to solve problems whose 
root causes lie outside the market itself. The stakeholder process has increasingly become the 
forum for debating broader questions of resource adequacy, economic development, 
infrastructure planning, transmission development, and state policy. That is not because those 
issues are fundamentally questions of market design, nor because stakeholder negotiations are 
the appropriate forum for resolving them. Rather, it is because no institution has been clearly 
accountable for addressing those issues before they reached PJM.  
By restoring clearer accountability for resource adequacy, much of that structural tension can be 
removed from the stakeholder process. PJM's markets can then focus on what competitive 
markets do exceptionally well: discovering efficient prices, facilitating competition, and 
allocating investment among competing resources. Likewise, stakeholders can return to what the 
process has always done best: improving implementation, refining market design, and applying 
their collective technical expertise to produce better solutions, rather than attempting to resolve 
broader institutional questions that markets alone cannot answer. 
This is the central institutional reform PJM now requires. The objective is not to replace 
competitive markets with centralized planning. It is to reconnect the obligation to serve load with 
the obligation to ensure that adequate resources exist to serve that load. Governance reforms can 
improve how decisions are made, but reconnecting responsibility for creating reliability 
obligations with responsibility for meeting them addresses why so many governance debates 
have become increasingly difficult in the first place. For more than twenty years, resource 
adequacy has largely been treated as something PJM procures on behalf of the region. I believe 
the next evolution of organized markets should instead treat resource adequacy as a shared 
institutional responsibility, with clearer accountability placed on the entities creating new 
reliability obligations. 
The guiding principle is straightforward: every decision that predictably creates a future 
reliability obligation should be accompanied by a credible plan for meeting that obligation. That 
principle begins with wholesale load-serving entities because they undertake the obligation to 
serve load. Before undertaking the obligation to serve load, an LSE should demonstrate a 
credible path for satisfying the resource adequacy requirements associated with that service.

Importantly, this is not simply a new obligation on LSEs. It also creates a stronger connection 
between wholesale resource adequacy and the state regulatory decisions that increasingly shape 
the future resource mix. 
This approach also clarifies the respective responsibilities of PJM, the states, and load-serving 
entities. PJM should remain responsible for determining the region's resource adequacy 
requirements. Given the size, complexity, and interconnected nature of the PJM system, no other 
institution is capable of performing the regional analysis necessary to determine how much 
accredited capacity is required, where it is needed, and when it must be available. States should 
continue to determine how the utilities and competitive suppliers they regulate satisfy those 
obligations, whether through long-term contracts, utility-owned resources, bilateral purchases, 
self-supply, or other market-based approaches. The obligation of the load-serving entity is to 
demonstrate that sufficient accredited resources will be available to serve the load it has 
undertaken to supply. 
PJM's role should not end with establishing the reliability requirement. It should also verify that 
entities undertaking wholesale load obligations have demonstrated a credible path toward 
satisfying those obligations over an appropriate planning horizon. As the delivery year 
approaches, those demonstrations should become increasingly rigorous. By the delivery year, the 
obligation should be clear: an LSE should either demonstrate that it has secured sufficient 
accredited resources to serve its load or bear consequences. Those consequences should include 
meaningful financial penalties that compensate other market participants for the reliability and 
scarcity costs imposed by the shortfall, together with operational consequences designed to 
protect system reliability and reinforce accountability.   
This framework also reinforces the partnership between PJM and the states discussed above. It 
does not assign new legal responsibilities to the states or diminish their authority over resource 
policy, utility regulation, or economic development. Today, a state may appropriately encourage 
significant economic development, approve new large electricity customers, or adopt policies 
that accelerate the retirement of existing generation. Those decisions remain matters of state 
authority. But if the utilities or competitive suppliers serving that load are also responsible for 
demonstrating compliance with PJM's resource adequacy requirements, those same decisions 
will naturally be accompanied by planning for the resources needed to support them. Rather than 
asking PJM's centralized capacity market to reconcile those decisions after they have been made, 
responsibility begins moving upstream to the institutions creating the new reliability obligation.  
Importantly, this framework works equally well in both traditionally regulated and competitive 
retail markets. The obligation attaches to the entity undertaking wholesale load service, not to a 
particular retail market structure. States remain free to determine how that obligation is satisfied, 
whether through vertically integrated utilities, competitive suppliers, bilateral contracting, self-
supply, or other market-based approaches. The objective is not to prescribe procurement

decisions or diminish competition. It is to align authority, responsibility, and accountability while 
preserving competitive markets.  
Viewed from that perspective, this evolution strengthens rather than diminishes PJM's role. PJM 
should continue doing what only a regional transmission organization can do: establish regional 
and locational resource adequacy requirements, administer transparent competitive markets, plan 
the transmission system, operate the bulk electric system, evaluate emerging reliability risks, and 
enforce compliance with regional reliability requirements. Reliability should no longer be treated 
as something PJM delivers on behalf of everyone else. It should become a shared obligation of 
the institutions whose decisions determine the future needs of the system.  
 
Five Principles for Strengthening the Regional Compact 
The recommendations in this statement can be distilled into five practical principles. None 
requires abandoning competitive markets or fundamentally restructuring PJM. Together, 
however, they would better align governance with the realities of today's electric system while 
preserving the regional compact that has served consumers well for more than two decades. 
1. Empower the Board to Lead 
The Board should clearly define strategic priorities, establish the objectives stakeholder 
processes are intended to achieve, set reasonable timelines for action, and be prepared to exercise 
its independent judgment when consensus cannot be reached. Consensus should remain the 
preferred outcome, but it should not become a prerequisite for leadership. That independence 
should also be reflected in Board structure. PJM should consider longer Board terms, coupled 
with an expectation that members generally serve a single term, to ensure that Board members 
can exercise independent judgment without concern that difficult but necessary decisions may 
affect their continued service. 
2. Institutionalize State Partnership 
The most significant planning initiatives, particularly those involving transmission planning and 
resource adequacy should be developed by PJM in collaboration with a standing committee of 
state representatives before entering the stakeholder process. States should determine how they 
are represented, and they should have access to the technical resources necessary to participate as 
effective partners. 
3. Align Responsibility for Resource Adequacy 
The obligation to serve wholesale load should be accompanied by a demonstrated plan for 
meeting the resource adequacy obligations that accompany that load with increasingly rigorous 
demonstrations as the delivery year approaches. This approach does not require re-regulation or

diminish competitive markets. Rather, it better aligns responsibility for creating new reliability 
obligations with responsibility for ensuring those obligations can be met. 
4. Plan Earlier Because Infrastructure Takes Longer 
The defining challenge of the next decade is no longer attracting capital. It is ensuring that 
generation, transmission, and other critical infrastructure can be planned, permitted, 
interconnected, and constructed before reliability needs arise. Every institution participating in 
the regional compact should evaluate its decisions through that lens. Better planning cannot 
eliminate infrastructure challenges, but it can ensure the region begins solving them before 
reliability is threatened. 
5. Let Markets and Stakeholders Do What They Do Best 
Competitive markets should be responsible for allocating investment among competing 
resources, not for correcting planning failures or reconciling decisions made outside the market. 
Likewise, the stakeholder process should focus on improving implementation and market design, 
not on resolving structural questions of resource policy, infrastructure development, and 
economic growth that require broader institutional leadership. By restoring accountability for 
resource adequacy and engaging the right institutions earlier, PJM can free both the market and 
the stakeholder process to perform the functions they were designed to perform. 
 
Conclusion 
The questions before the Commission extend well beyond the governance of a single regional 
transmission organization. They concern the future of regional coordination itself. 
For more than two decades, PJM has demonstrated that states can retain authority over their own 
energy policies while participating in regional institutions that improve reliability, lower costs, 
and support efficient wholesale markets. That achievement should not be taken for granted. It 
remains one of the most important institutional accomplishments in modern electricity policy. 
The pressures confronting PJM today are real, but they are not evidence that the regional model 
has failed. They reflect an electric system that has changed more rapidly than the institutions 
designed to support it. The answer, therefore, is not to weaken the regional compact. It is to 
strengthen it. 
That means a Board with the confidence to provide strategic leadership while remaining 
informed by stakeholder expertise. It means a more meaningful partnership between PJM and the 
states. It means planning earlier because infrastructure now determines the pace at which 
reliability can be maintained. And it means reconnecting the obligation to serve load with 
accountability for ensuring that sufficient accredited resources exist to serve it.

If we can restore that alignment, many of the governance debates now consuming PJM will 
become more manageable because the market, the stakeholder process, the Board, and the states 
will each be focused on the responsibilities they are uniquely positioned to perform.  
Ultimately, preserving the regional compact is not about changing who has the loudest voice in 
the stakeholder process. It is about ensuring that every institution entrusted with responsibility 
for the electric system has the authority, accountability, and confidence to fulfill the role only it 
can perform. 
If we accomplish that, we will do more than improve PJM's governance. We will preserve one of 
the nation's most successful regional institutions while ensuring it is prepared for the challenges 
of the next generation of the electric system. 
Thank you, and I look forward to participating in the Commission's discussion.
